summary: Discusses the threats to protocols that carry authentication for network access and the security requirements that follow, as input for the PANA working group's design.

plainLanguage.summary: Before a device can use a network, it has to log in, and anything on the same link can try to interfere. This memo lists what could go wrong at each step of that login and turns the list into rules the protocol must follow.

subtitle: The attacks a network-access login protocol must survive, and the eight rules that come out of them.

tldr.problem: A device that wants access to a network has no prior trust with the network's authentication agent, and on a shared link other machines can spoof, replay, hijack or steal the service.
tldr.mechanism: The memo walks through each stage of access, from finding the agent to leaving the network, listing the threats that apply and whether they need a shared link, then turns each one into a requirement.
tldr.outcome: The eight requirements, covering mutual authentication, key establishment, replay protection and protected disconnect messages, were written as input for the PANA working group's protocol design.

today: RFC 4016 is an Informational memo published in March 2005, and the metadata records no obsoleting or updating RFC. It was written as input to the PANA working group's design, so it states requirements rather than defining a protocol.

sections.title: Why a Threat Analysis Comes First
sections.content:
The Protocol for Carrying Authentication for Network Access (PANA) working group is building methods for authenticating clients to an access network using IP-based protocols. This memo does not design that protocol. It lists the threats such a protocol has to survive and turns them into requirements the working group can design against.

Getting access takes several steps. A client first discovers the IP address of the PANA authentication agent, then runs an authentication protocol to prove itself to the network. After that, more messages may be exchanged over the life of the access session. The threats that apply to each step are discussed separately. The requirement wording used throughout is that PANA must be able to prevent a given threat, meaning the protocol should be capable of preventing it; whether a deployment actually uses the feature that does so is a separate choice.
sections.plainLanguage: Before a device can use a network, it has to log in. This memo lists what could go wrong at each step of that login and turns the list into rules the protocol must follow.

sections.title: The Parties and What They Trust
sections.content:
The PANA exchange involves four roles. The PANA client (PaC) is the entity in the edge subnet that wants access, tied to a device and to the credentials that prove its identity. The PANA authentication agent (PAA) authenticates that client and grants network access service. The authentication server (AS) does the authenticating, and may sit with the PAA or in the back end. The enforcement point (EP) is the node that filters the client's packets using the device identifier the PAA has authorized.

Not all of these start out trusting each other. The PAA and the AS share a trust relationship, and their conversation is protected by a static or dynamic security association; the threats on that path are covered elsewhere. The PAA and the EP are in the same administrative domain, so the operator can protect the traffic between them. The PaC and the AS are also in the same administrative domain and share a trust relationship.

The PaC and the PAA normally belong to two different administrative domains and do not necessarily share trust at the start. They establish a security association in the process of authentication, and every message between them is subject to the threats this memo lists. The PaC and the EP do not share trust either, but keys established during authentication can later secure the link between them.
sections.plainLanguage: Four parties take part. The client asks for access, the agent checks its identity, the server holds the credentials, and the enforcement point decides which packets to let through. Only some of them trust each other from the start.

sections.title: Shared Links and Dedicated Links
sections.content:
PANA is meant for environments where there is no prior trust relationship or security association between the client and the other nodes. Two features of those environments shape the threat model. The link between the PaC and the PAA may be a shared medium such as Ethernet, or it may not be shared, as on a DSL network. And all the PaCs may be authenticated to the access network at layer 2, for example in a 3GPP2 CDMA network, sharing a security association with a layer 2 authentication agent such as a base transceiver station.

Even in that second case the clients still do not trust each other. Any one of them can pretend to be a PAA, spoof IP addresses and launch various other attacks. Throughout the memo, a link that is not shared is assumed to be physically secure. If that assumption cannot be made, the link has to be treated as the same as a link shared by more than one node.
sections.plainLanguage: Some networks give each customer their own dedicated line. Others share one cable or one radio channel between many customers. The attacks in this memo mostly need a shared link, so the difference matters.

sections.title: Threats at Each Stage
sections.content:
The threats are grouped by the stage the client is at. In discovery, a malicious node can pretend to be a PAA by sending a spoofed advertisement. Because a spoofed advertisement can advertise weaker authentication methods than the real PAA supports, this opens the door to a bidding down attack. Discovery is hard to protect, because the PaC and the PAA have no prior trust relationship.

In authentication, an attacker can send a false success or failure message, either to keep the client out of the network or to cut the exchange short. A man-in-the-middle attack is possible when the client and the agent both believe they are talking to each other while both are talking to the attacker. If compound authentication methods are used, the attacker can tunnel the identity of the legitimate client unless the methods are cryptographically bound to each other. Replayed messages can create false successes or failures later. The device identifier attack goes further: the attacker impersonates a PAA, rewrites the IP source address of the packets and fixes the UDP or TCP checksum, and ends up with the access granted for its own address.

In leaving, a fake PAA can revoke access, a fake client can send a disconnect message, and a client can vanish without warning, for example when a cable is unplugged. In service theft, an attacker spoofs the IP and MAC addresses of an authorized client, which is easy because it takes only sniffing the wire, and gets service for free. In communication between the PAA and the EP, an attacker can eavesdrop on the access control information or impersonate the PAA to the enforcement point. The memo also lists miscellaneous attacks: denial of service against the PAA or AS, including flooding it with authentication requests to exhaust memory and forcing expensive computations to exhaust CPU; and attacks on address assignment, where clients that receive an address before authenticating can exhaust the address space or answer every duplicate address detection query to block allocation to others.
sections.plainLanguage: The threats are listed by stage: finding the agent, logging in, leaving, stealing someone else's service, and the path between the agent and the network edge. Each stage gets its own requirement later.

sections.title: The Eight Requirements
sections.content:
The threats are converted into eight requirements. The discovery process cannot be assumed to be protected. The protocol must be able to mutually authenticate the PaC and the PAA and to establish keys between them to protect the messages. When compound authentication methods are used, the methods must be cryptographically bound. The protocol must be able to resist replay attacks. It must protect the device identifier against spoofing as it is exchanged between the PaC and the PAA. It must protect disconnect and revocation messages, and it must not depend on the PaC sending a disconnect message at all, because the client can disappear without warning.

The last two requirements cover the network side. The authenticated session must be bound securely to the device identifier of the client, so that service theft is prevented, and the protocol must be able to bootstrap a shared secret between the PaC and the PAA that can later be used to set up a security association between the PaC and the EP. The communication between the PAA and the EP must be protected against eavesdropping and spoofing attacks.
sections.plainLanguage: Eight rules come out of the threat list. They cover logging in properly, protecting the client's address, surviving replays, and keeping the agent and the network edge talking safely to each other.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The memo treats shared and unshared links separately, but it says that in practice the distinction may be difficult to make. A dial-up link may be a point-to-point IP tunnel, for example. For most of the threats in the document, the link should therefore be assumed to be a shared link.
sections.plainLanguage: In real networks it is often hard to tell a dedicated link from a shared one. So for most of these threats, assume anyone on the link can listen.

viz.caption: THE STEPS TO GET NETWORK ACCESS, ILLUSTRATIVE (RFC 4016)

messages.label: Solicitation
messages.note: The client looks for the PANA authentication agent, or waits for advertisements.

messages.label: Advertisement
messages.note: The agent announces itself. A malicious node can send a spoofed advertisement.

messages.label: Authentication exchange
messages.note: The client proves its identity, and the agent can prove its own.

messages.label: Credential check
messages.note: If the agent cannot read the credentials, it checks them with the server in the home realm.

messages.label: Access control information
messages.note: The agent tells the enforcement point which device identifier to allow.

items.title: Discovery
items.text: A malicious node pretends to be the agent with a spoofed advertisement, and may try to make the client pick a weaker authentication method.

items.title: Authentication
items.text: False success or failure messages, a man-in-the-middle, replayed messages and a spoofed device identifier.

items.title: Leaving
items.text: A fake agent revokes access, a fake client sends a disconnect, and a real client can vanish without warning.

items.title: Service theft
items.text: An attacker spoofs the IP and MAC addresses of an authorized client to get service for free.

items.title: Agent to enforcement point
items.text: An attacker eavesdrops on the access control information, or impersonates the agent to the enforcement point.

items.title: Miscellaneous
items.text: Denial of service against the agent or the server, and attacks on address assignment before authentication.

cells: Must not assume that the discovery process is protected.
Must be able to mutually authenticate the client and the agent, and establish keys between them to protect the messages.
Must cryptographically bind compound authentication methods when they are used.
Must be able to protect itself against replay attacks.
Must protect the device identifier against spoofing between the client and the agent.
Must protect disconnect and revocation messages, and must not depend on the client sending a disconnect message.
Must bind the authenticated session to the device identifier, and bootstrap a shared secret that can secure the link to the enforcement point.
Must protect the communication between the agent and the enforcement point against eavesdropping and spoofing.
